endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: Relevant testing may include multi-turn simulated encounters that assess time to escalation in evolving presentations, the quality of escalation language and handoff information

endorsements.title: It Is the Journey, Not the Destination: Moving From End Points to Trajectories When Assessing Chatbot Mental Health Safety
endorsements.quote: To be clinically relevant, shorter experimental windows need calibration against these longer trajectories, for example, through periodic extended dialogue sessions, sliding-window analyses, or full context analyses of real transcripts.

endorsements.title: An Acceptance Criteria Framework for Determining the Implementation Fit of Custom Large Language Models in Public Health Interventions
endorsements.quote: However, for off-topic prompts, “nonproblematic” primarily means the custom LLM does not provide out-of-scope guidance and instead redirects users to the custom model’s intended topic and resources.

evidence.title: Toward Trustworthy Chatbots: A Protocol for Red Teaming for Health Related Conversations
evidence.outcome: multi-turn behavioral adherence testing
evidence.effect: Multi-turn testing found vulnerabilities single-turn missed; advice_query BA errors reached 50% (5/10) and user_distress 40% (4/10).
evidence.quote: Furthermore, multi-turn stress tests revealed critical vulnerabilities that single-turn testing missed, directly informing our choice of targeted mitigations.

evidence.title: Fine-Tuning, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and Hybrid Large Language Models for Postoperative Decision Support: Comparative Analysis
evidence.outcome: Refusal of out-of-scope queries with vs without scope/refusal instructions
evidence.effect: Baseline refused 0/30 out-of-scope queries; FT 30/30, RAG 27/30, hybrid 30/30 with explicit refusal instructions. Authors note this reflects prompt compliance on previewed queries, not generalizable boundary recognition. Single-turn only.
evidence.quote: Accordingly, these findings primarily reflect compliance with predefined refusal instructions on previewed safety-query types rather than intrinsic or generalizable boundary-recognition ability.
evidence.sample_unit: held-out expert-authored patient-style postoperative queries (per model configuration)

evidence.title: Development of a Guideline-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation Chatbot Referencing Web-Based Cancer Clinical Practice Guidelines
evidence.outcome: Chatbot declining out-of-scope cancer-type questions
evidence.effect: For out-of-scope questions, the chatbot consistently declined to answer and indicated that the available information was insufficient.
evidence.quote: For out-of-scope questions, the chatbot consistently declined to answer and indicated that the available information was insufficient.

evidence.title: RESPECT: a conversational AI system for informed consent with accuracy, safety, and stakeholder-centered evaluation
evidence.outcome: Whether the conversational AI declines out-of-scope/inappropriate questions in adversarial simulation
evidence.effect: RESPECT appropriate refusal 0.97 vs Direct Prompting 0.90 (p<0.05); utility 0.69 vs 1.00. Single-turn questions only, not multi-turn.
evidence.quote: RESPECT achieved an appropriate refusal rate of 0.97 and utility of 0.69, significantly outperforming Direct Prompting in appropriate refusal (0.90, p < 0.05) while Direct Prompting achieved perfect utility (1.00, p < 0.05).
evidence.sample_unit: questions (100 adversarial attack questions plus 36 legitimate questions)

evidence.title: Development and Validation of CPX-MATE: An End-to-End Medical Education Platform Integrating Voice-Based Virtual Patient Simulation and Automated Real-time Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Virtual patient dialogue error types (tangential, oversharing, role-breaking, off-script) by speech-to-speech configuration
evidence.effect: Overall error rates were 1.77% (full-capacity) vs 9.43% (resource-limited) across 3,282 turns (p<0.001), driven by tangential and oversharing responses; no off-script errors.
evidence.quote: Across 3,282 dialogue turns, overall error rates were 1.77% versus 9.43% for full-capacity versus resource-limited STS configurations (p<0.001), driven by fewer tangential and oversharing responses; no off-script errors were observed.

evidence.title: Substance-induced manic psychosis in which delusions were corroborated by a chatbot - case report
evidence.outcome: Whether a general-purpose chatbot gave medical advice beyond appropriate scope
evidence.effect: Single case: the chatbot gave medical advice, including discouragement of prescribed antipsychotic medication, conflicting with clinical recommendations.
evidence.quote: This case demonstrates that, in patients with psychotic symptoms, AI chatbots may reinforce delusional beliefs and impair the development of insight, and may also interfere with engagement with treatment by providing advice that conflicts with clinical recommendations.

evidence.title: The Slow Drift of Support: Boundary Failures in Multi-Turn Mental Health LLM Dialogues
evidence.outcome: Boundary violations (guarantees, assuming responsibility, professional roles) by mental health LLMs over multi-turn dialogues
evidence.effect: Violations were common under both static progression and adaptive probing with similar rates. Adaptive probing cut mean turns to first boundary crossing from 9.21 to 4.64. Definitive or zero-risk promises were the main breach.
evidence.quote: The experimental results show that violations are common, and both pressure modes produced similar violation rates.

evidence.title: Do No Harm: Exposing Hidden Vulnerabilities of LLMs via Persona-based Client Simulation Attack in Psychological Counseling
evidence.outcome: LLM safety failures (unauthorized medical advice, reinforcing delusions) under persona-driven multi-turn counseling attacks
evidence.effect: PCSA substantially outperformed four baselines on seven LLMs. Models gave unauthorized medical advice, reinforced delusions, and implicitly encouraged risky actions. No numbers in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Our results reveal that current LLMs remain vulnerable to domain-specific adversarial tactics, providing unauthorized medical advice, reinforcing delusions, and implicitly encouraging risky actions.

evidence.title: Toward Trustworthy Chatbots: A Protocol for Red Teaming for Health Related Conversations
evidence.outcome: Behavioral adherence errors (scope/safety rule violations) in single- and multi-turn attacks
evidence.effect: Single-turn BA error rate 15% (12/80); advice_query BA errors rose to 50% (5/10) in multi-turn tests and user_distress to 40% (4/10).
evidence.quote: In multi-turn stress tests, error rates rose sharply under conversational persistence: advice_query BA errors reached 50% (5/10) and user_distress reached 40% (4/10), accounting for all high-severity errors (4/4).

evidence.title: The Ability of AI Therapy Bots to Set Limits With Distressed Adolescents: Simulation-Based Comparison Study
evidence.outcome: Rate at which chatbots endorsed harmful or ill-advised proposals from fictional adolescents
evidence.effect: Chatbots actively endorsed harmful proposals in 19 of 60 (32%) opportunities; 4 of 10 endorsed half or more; none opposed all.
evidence.quote: Across 60 total scenarios, chatbots actively endorsed harmful proposals in 19 out of the 60 (32%) opportunities to do so.
evidence.sample_unit: chatbot responses to scenarios (10 chatbots x 6 proposals)

evidence.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Chatbots for Parental Guidance in Pediatric Orthopaedics: A Pilot Feasibility Study
evidence.outcome: Unprompted treatment recommendations beyond educational scope, rated by clinician evaluators
evidence.effect: No hallucinations identified; 88.9% of evaluators confirmed absence of unprompted treatment recommendations.
evidence.quote: No hallucinations were identified, and 88.9% of evaluators confirmed the absence of unprompted treatment recommendations.

evidence.title: Fine-Tuning, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and Hybrid Large Language Models for Postoperative Decision Support: Comparative Analysis
evidence.outcome: out-of-scope refusal accuracy
evidence.effect: Baseline 0/30; FT 30/30; RAG 27/30; RAG+FT 30/30; overall P≤.001.
evidence.quote: Enhanced models also demonstrated higher safety or refusal accuracy than baseline; however, the baseline configuration did not receive equivalent safety or deferral instructions, which likely influenced these findings.
evidence.sample_unit: held-out expert-authored patient-style postoperative queries (per model configuration)

evidence.title: Patient-Facing AI Chatbot Treatment-Direction Advice in Orthodontic Health Communication: A Scenario-Based Comparison with Expert Consensus
evidence.outcome: Chatbot advice concordance with expert benchmark and coded safety concerns in orthodontic treatment-direction scenarios
evidence.effect: Exact concordance was 82.5% ChatGPT, 67.5% Claude, 42.5% Copilot, 37.5% Gemini; coded safety-concern rates ranged from 15.0% to 62.5%; chatbots gave appliance-direction advice.
evidence.quote: Coded safety-concern rates ranged from 15.0% to 62.5%.
evidence.sample_unit: chatbot first responses (40 scenarios x 4 chatbots)

evidence.title: ArGen: Auto-Regulation of Generative AI via GRPO and Policy-as-Code
evidence.outcome: Domain-scope adherence of medical AI assistant versus baseline model
evidence.effect: 70.9% improvement in domain-scope adherence over the baseline, implying the baseline model had substantial out-of-scope behavior.
evidence.quote: This challenging application demonstrates ArGen's adaptability, achieving a 70.9% improvement in domain-scope adherence over the baseline.

evidence.title: MultiTurnPSB: Evaluating Multi-Turn Jailbreak Attacks an dClassifier-Based Defenses for Medical AI Safety
evidence.outcome: Unsafe response rate across four adversarial turns under live attack
evidence.effect: Unsafe responses rose from 35% to nearly 80% by Turn 4 under live attack; GPT-4.1-mini and Claude Sonnet 4.5 diverged to a 19x gap by Turn 4.
evidence.quote: Unsafe responses rise from 35% to nearly 80% by Turn 4 under live attack.

evidence.title: TAF-MED: Multi-Turn Safety Refusal Collapse in LLMs Under Declared Self-Treatment Intent
evidence.outcome: Medication-safety boundary persistence across multi-turn conversations after declared self-treatment intent
evidence.effect: 71.6% of conversations contained an UNSAFE response; 61.4% of those beginning with a strictly SAFE response later collapsed to UNSAFE; model-level collapse rates ranged from 24.4% to 96.2%.
evidence.quote: Overall, 71.6% of conversations contained an UNSAFE response, and 61.4% of those beginning with a strictly SAFE response later collapsed to UNSAFE; model-level collapse rates ranged from 24.4% to 96.2%.

evidence.title: Vertical Model Paradox: Systemic Ethical Blind Spots in Domain-Specific Medical AI
evidence.outcome: Safe refusal of high-risk requests within intended-use boundaries
evidence.effect: Models passed only 52.38% of prompts on safely refusing high-risk physical therapy procedures.
evidence.quote: Notably, models exhibited severe vulnerabilities in maintaining clinical traceability for medical records (pass rate 47.62%) and safely refusing high-risk physical therapy procedures (52.38%), consistently lacking emergency fail-safes and upfront regulatory disclaimers.

evidence.title: Cannot, Should Not, Did Anyway: Benchmarking Constraint Enforcement Failure in Frontier LLMs
evidence.outcome: Model stays within intended-use boundaries and declines requests under pressure
evidence.effect: Models often recognize a request should be refused yet comply when surrounding instructions exert sufficient pressure; refusal robustness is context-dependent.
evidence.quote: We show that this obscures a critical failure mode: models often recognize that a request should be refused, yet comply when the surrounding instructions exert sufficient pressure.

evidence.title: Red-Teaming Medical AI: Systematic Adversarial Evaluation of LLM Safety Guardrails in Clinical Contexts
evidence.outcome: Multi-turn escalation attack success rate against the medical assistant
evidence.effect: Multi-turn escalation attacks achieved 0% success (0/20), while authority impersonation prompts elicited harmful responses in 45.0% of cases.
evidence.quote: Multi-turn escalation attacks achieved 0% success (0/20).

evidence.title: Robustness of a Large Language Model (LLM)-Based Virtual Patient for Japanese History-Taking Training Under Direct and Indirect Instructional Contamination
evidence.outcome: Forbidden information leakage and role drift of virtual patient LLM within intended role boundaries
evidence.effect: Forbidden leakage ~0.60 events per episode in clean condition (95% CI 0.502-0.698); role drift not observed; refusal/clarification 0.
evidence.quote: However, forbidden information leakage occurred at approximately 0.60 events per episode under the clean condition (0.600; 95% CI, 0.502-0.698), indicating incomplete constraint adherence despite high case fidelity.

commentary.bottom_line: Four offline studies suggest chatbots can be configured to decline out-of-scope questions, and one found that multi-turn probes exposed errors that single-turn tests missed. No study shows that this testing reduces out-of-scope advice reaching patients in real deployments.

perspectives.view: Four studies test scope-refusal behavior, and all are offline or simulated at evidence levels 4 and 5. Only one compared multi-turn with single-turn testing, and it used 20 multi-turn probes. Two others used single-turn questions only, and the Japanese study did not report its turn structure. Small samples, indirect settings, and absent patient outcomes support very low certainty.

In one test, multi-turn probes raised advice-query adherence errors to 50% (5/10), against an overall single-turn error rate of 15% (12/80). Hazard benchmarks point the same way. In one, 61.4% of conversations that began safely later became unsafe. In another, unsafe responses rose from 35% to nearly 80% by turn 4. Single-turn evaluation may miss these late failures.

A model without scope instructions refused 0 of 30 out-of-scope queries, while tuned versions refused 27 to 30 of 30. The authors attribute this result to prompt compliance on previewed queries. Another system raised appropriate refusal from 0.90 to 0.97 but lowered utility from 1.00 to 0.69. Evaluation may need to measure over-refusal alongside declines.

In a South Korean virtual patient deployment, error rates across 3,282 turns were 1.77% with a full-capacity speech configuration and 9.43% with a resource-limited one. This suggests that scope test results may not carry over between configurations, so teams may need to retest after each change. No study reports the staff time or cost of multi-turn testing.

None of the four tests enrolled or simulated Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. Hazard studies in non-English settings found safety-concern rates of 15.0% to 62.5% in Turkish orthodontic scenarios. A Japanese virtual patient benchmark found forbidden information leakage of about 0.60 events per episode. Scope behavior for these users remains untested.

A regulatory discussion paper states that relevant testing may include multi-turn simulated encounters that assess time to escalation and the quality of handoff information. The wording is permissive and does not set a requirement. None of the supplied studies measured time to escalation, so the evidence does not yet show how testing would meet that expectation.

One case report describes a general-purpose chatbot that discouraged a patient's prescribed antipsychotic medication. In scenarios posed by fictional adolescents, chatbots endorsed harmful proposals in 19 of 60 (32%) opportunities. No included test measured whether a chatbot that declined a request then directed the user to a human or another resource, which affects patient trust and access to care.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployed conversational systems that underwent multi-turn scope testing with systems that did not, using outcomes such as out-of-scope advice reaching patients, time to escalation, redirection to a human, or over-refusal of legitimate questions. Of the existing tests, two used single-turn questions only, one used 20 multi-turn probes, and one did not report its turn structure; all were offline, and none reported the testing burden.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the four studies that test the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Two hazard studies in Turkish and Japanese settings suggest that scope and safety failures occur in non-English use. Health systems serving these populations therefore have no direct evidence that scope testing performs as intended for their patients.
